lines.text: Let go of a probe at the hundred-kilometre line, and watch the speed.
This is our own simple model: a hundred-kilogram probe, sixty centimetres wide, falling straight down.
At eighty kilometres, it's moving at six hundred and eighteen metres a second.
At sixty, eight hundred and seventy-four. At fifty, nine hundred and seventy-two.
At forty kilometres, a hundred and twelve seconds after the drop, it reaches one thousand and forty-three metres a second.
That's Mach three point three, because sound up there travels at only about three hundred and seventeen.
The real record fall, Baumgartner's, reached Mach one point two five. Our probe is going more than twice as fast.
And it's still speeding up as it passes forty kilometres. There are forty kilometres left to the ground.
So does the probe hit the ground at Mach three? The full video on our channel has the answer. Like and subscribe so you don't miss the next one.
lines.cue: caption: HITS THE GROUND AT MACH 3?
